paper_title: Contributions of insula and superior temporal sulcus to interpersonal guilt and responsibility in social decisions

claims.claim: Feelings of interpersonal guilt and responsibility evoked by social decisions involve neural mechanisms in humans.

evidence_by_agent.results: This study investigated the neural mechanisms involved in feelings of interpersonal guilt and responsibility evoked by social decisions in humans.

claims.claim: Participants’ happiness decreases following both low lottery outcomes for themselves and for their partner.

evidence_by_agent.results: As expected, participant happiness decreased following both low lottery outcomes for themselves and for the partner.

claims.claim: Happiness decreases following low outcomes for the partner are larger when the participant rather than their partner had made the choice.

evidence_by_agent.results: Crucially, happiness decreases following low outcomes for the partner were larger when the participant rather than their partner had made the choice, which fits an operational definition of guilt.
evidence_by_agent.caption: Crucially, responsibility for low lottery outcomes for the partner decreased participant happiness more than the same outcomes following partner choices (see Results), which fits the definition of interpersonal guilt.

claims.claim: The guilt effect is associated with BOLD signal increase in the left anterior insula.

evidence_by_agent.results: This guilt effect was associated with BOLD signal increase in the left anterior insula.

claims.claim: Connectivity between the left anterior insula and the right inferior frontal gyrus varies depending on choice and experimental condition.

evidence_by_agent.results: Connectivity between this region and the right inferior frontal gyrus varied depending on choice and experimental condition, suggesting that this part of prefrontal cortex is sensitive to guilt-related information during social choices.

claims.claim: A left superior temporal sulcus cluster tracks partner reward prediction errors that follow participant choices.

evidence_by_agent.results: A model-based analysis revealed a left superior temporal sulcus cluster that tracked partner reward prediction errors that followed participant choices.

claims.claim: Participants’ momentary happiness correlates with rewards obtained by themselves and their partners.

evidence_by_agent.results: Across all trials, in both studies, participant momentary happiness correlated with rewards obtained in the current trial by the participant and by the partner.
evidence_by_agent.caption: Happiness varied with rewards received by the participant ( A, E ).

claims.claim: Participant happiness is lower when they chose the lottery for the partner, independent of the outcome.

evidence_by_agent.results: Happiness varied depending on the participant’s agency (Social + Solo vs. Partner), and found happiness to be lower when the participant chose, independent of the outcome.

claims.claim: Participants felt worse following low lottery outcomes for the partner if those outcomes were consequences of their own choice rather than the partner’s.

evidence_by_agent.results: When the partner received the low lottery outcome, participant happiness was lower when they rather than the partner had chosen the lottery.
evidence_by_agent.caption: Crucially, responsibility for low lottery outcomes for the partner decreased participant happiness more than the same outcomes following partner choices (see Results), which fits the definition of interpersonal guilt.

claims.claim: Participants’ happiness was influenced by the outcomes of choices for their partner, especially by outcomes resulting from participant decisions.

evidence_by_agent.results: In sum, in both studies, we found evidence that participants’ happiness was influenced by the outcomes of choices for their partner, especially by outcomes resulting from participant decisions.

claims.claim: The precuneus and left temporo-parietal junction are most active when participants choose the lottery in the Social condition.

evidence_by_agent.results: Only the precuneus and TPJ showed positive differences in both comparisons, indicating that these regions were most active when participants chose the lottery in the Social condition.
evidence_by_agent.caption: Coefficients of linear mixed models (LMMs) indicate that two of these regions, precuneus and TPJ, were most active when participants chose the lottery in the Social condition.

claims.claim: Activation in the insulae increases in situations during which participants experienced guilt for low outcomes impacting their partner.

evidence_by_agent.results: Thus, activation in our insula ROIs increased in situations during which participants experienced guilt for low outcomes impacting their partner, compared to similar outcomes resulting from the partner’s choices.

claims.claim: A cluster within the left superior temporal sulcus tracks partner reward prediction errors resulting from participant rather than partner choices.

evidence_by_agent.results: We found this effect in one cluster within the left STS (p FWE = 0.022, T = 4.70, d = 0.53, Z = 4.57, 100 voxels, peak at MNI [−52 –32 0]).
evidence_by_agent.caption: Within brain regions sensitive to outcomes of risky choices, one cluster in the left superior temporal sulcus region showed a higher response to partner reward prediction errors resulting from participant rather than partner choices.

claims.claim: Participants chose the risky option slightly more often in the Solo condition than in the Social condition in Study 1.

evidence_by_agent.caption: Participants chose the risky option slightly more often in the Solo condition than in the Social condition in Study 1.

claims.claim: Participants did not choose the risky option more often in the Solo condition than in the Social condition in Study 2.

evidence_by_agent.caption: Participants chose the risky option slightly more often in the Solo condition than in the Social condition in Study 1 ( A ) but not in Study 2 ( D ).

claims.claim: Risk premiums did not differ between Solo and Social conditions in Study 1.

evidence_by_agent.caption: Risk premiums did not differ between Solo and Social conditions.

claims.claim: Risk premiums did not differ between Solo and Social conditions in Study 2.

evidence_by_agent.caption: Risk premiums did not differ between Solo and Social conditions.

claims.claim: Participants were slightly more risk averse in the Social than in the Solo condition in Study 1.

evidence_by_agent.caption: Participants were slightly more risk averse in the Social than in the Solo condition in Study 1 only.

claims.claim: Participants’ risk aversion did not differ significantly between Solo and Social conditions in Study 2.

evidence_by_agent.caption: Values of the risk aversion parameter ρ in the Solo and Social conditions were broadly consistent with Risk premium values, but showed that participants were slightly more risk averse in the Social than in the Solo condition in Study 1 only.

claims.notes: The caption does not explicitly state that risk aversion did not differ in Study 2, but implies it by contrasting with Study 1.

claims.claim: Happiness varied with rewards received by the participant in Study 1.

evidence_by_agent.caption: Happiness varied with rewards received by the participant ( A, E ).

claims.claim: Happiness varied with rewards received by the participant in Study 2.

evidence_by_agent.caption: Happiness varied with rewards received by the participant ( A, E ).

claims.claim: Happiness varied with rewards received by the partner in Study 1.

evidence_by_agent.caption: Happiness varied with rewards received by the partner ( B, F ).

claims.claim: Happiness varied with rewards received by the partner in Study 2.

evidence_by_agent.caption: Happiness varied with rewards received by the partner ( B, F ).

claims.claim: A computational model predicted variations in participants’ momentary happiness well in Study 1.

evidence_by_agent.caption: A computational model taking into account expected, previous and current rewards, reward prediction errors for both participant and partner, and decision-maker (Responsibility Redux model, see Results) predicted the variations in participants’ momentary happiness well ( C, G , and  Table 1 ).

claims.claim: A computational model predicted variations in participants’ momentary happiness well in Study 2.

evidence_by_agent.caption: A computational model taking into account expected, previous and current rewards, reward prediction errors for both participant and partner, and decision-maker (Responsibility Redux model, see Results) predicted the variations in participants’ momentary happiness well ( C, G , and  Table 1 ).

claims.claim: Responsibility for low lottery outcomes for the partner decreased participant happiness more than the same outcomes following partner choices in Study 1.

evidence_by_agent.caption: Crucially, responsibility for low lottery outcomes for the partner decreased participant happiness more than the same outcomes following partner choices (see Results), which fits the definition of interpersonal guilt.

claims.claim: Responsibility for low lottery outcomes for the partner decreased participant happiness more than the same outcomes following partner choices in Study 2.

evidence_by_agent.caption: Crucially, responsibility for low lottery outcomes for the partner decreased participant happiness more than the same outcomes following partner choices (see Results), which fits the definition of interpersonal guilt.

claims.claim: Regions showing a greater response when participants chose the risky option rather than the safe option, irrespective of Social or Solo condition.

evidence_by_agent.caption: Regions showing a greater response when participants chose the risky (lottery) rather than the safe option, irrespective of Social or Solo condition.

claims.claim: Regions showing a greater response when participants chose for both themselves and their partner rather than just for themselves (Social > Solo).

evidence_by_agent.caption: Regions showing a greater response when participants chose for both themselves and their partner rather than just for themselves (Social > Solo).

claims.claim: Precuneus and TPJ were most active when participants chose the lottery in the Social condition.

evidence_by_agent.results: Only the precuneus and TPJ showed positive differences in both comparisons, indicating that these regions were most active when participants chose the lottery in the Social condition.
evidence_by_agent.caption: Coefficients of linear mixed models (LMMs) indicate that two of these regions, precuneus and TPJ, were most active when participants chose the lottery in the Social condition.

claims.claim: Brain regions more active during receipt of the outcomes of lotteries than safe choices (all conditions).

evidence_by_agent.caption: Brain regions more active during receipt of the outcomes of lotteries than safe choices (all conditions).

claims.claim: Insula ROIs mirrored the guilt effect observed in behavioural data: voxels responded more to low lottery outcomes (L) for the partner when these resulted from participant’s rather than the partner’s choices.

evidence_by_agent.caption: Coefficients of LMMs indicated that insula ROIs (see D) mirrored the guilt effect observed in our behavioural data: voxels here responded more to low lottery outcomes (L) for the partner when these resulted from participant’s rather than the partner’s choices, even when responses to high outcomes were subtracted (L–H).

claims.claim: A cluster of voxels within the left insula ROI showed higher responses to low lottery outcomes for the partner if these resulted from participant rather than partner choices.

evidence_by_agent.caption: A mass-univariate, voxel-wise analysis showed a compatible result: A cluster of voxels within the left insula ROI showed higher responses to low lottery outcomes for the partner if these resulted from participant rather than partner choices.

claims.claim: Activation in bilateral ventral striatum explained by a computational model-based regressor coding participant rewards.

evidence_by_agent.caption: Activation in bilateral ventral striatum explained by a computational model-based regressor coding participant rewards.

claims.claim: A cluster in the left superior temporal sulcus region showed a higher response to partner reward prediction errors resulting from participant rather than partner choices.

evidence_by_agent.results: We found this effect in one cluster within the left STS (p FWE = 0.022, T = 4.70, d = 0.53, Z = 4.57, 100 voxels, peak at MNI [−52 –32 0]).
evidence_by_agent.caption: Within brain regions sensitive to outcomes of risky choices, one cluster in the left superior temporal sulcus region showed a higher response to partner reward prediction errors resulting from participant rather than partner choices.

claims.claim: Response in this cluster to the computational-model-based regressors coding participant reward prediction resulting from participant and partner choices, for both sessions of the experiment.

evidence_by_agent.caption: Response in this cluster to the computational-model-based regressors coding participant reward prediction resulting from participant and partner choices, for both sessions of the experiment.

claims.claim: Functional connectivity between the left anterior insula (seed) and a cluster in the right inferior frontal gyrus at the time of the choice varied as a function of condition (Social vs. Solo) and choice (Risky or Safe).

evidence_by_agent.caption: Changes in functional connectivity between the left anterior insula (seed) and a cluster in the right inferior frontal gyrus at the time of the choice as a function of condition (Social vs. Solo) and choice (Risky or Safe).

claims.claim: Functional connectivity between the left STS (seed) and a cluster in the left inferior frontal gyrus was highest when participants made Safe choices for themselves and Risky choices for both players.

evidence_by_agent.caption: Connectivity between the left STS (seed) and a cluster in the left inferior frontal gyrus that did not survive corrections for multiple tests, where connectivity with the left STS (the seed region) showed the opposite pattern: connectivity was highest when participants made Safe choices for themselves and Risky choices for both players (p uncorrected  = 0.001,  T  = 4.44,  Z  = 4.30, 35 voxels, peak at MNI [–48 14 6]).

claims.claim: Parameter recovery for the Responsibility Redux model showed stable parameter estimates.

evidence_by_agent.caption: Stability of the estimated parameters of the temporal difference models was evaluated by attempting to recover parameters from synthetic data created using each participant’s real estimated parameters.

claims.notes: Panel describes methodological validation rather than a direct empirical claim.

claims.claim: The experiment was implemented in MATLAB using Psychtoolbox extensions.

evidence_by_agent.structure: It was implemented in MATLAB (Version R2016b; RRID: SCR_001622 ; The MathWorks, Inc, Natick, MA) using the Psychtoolbox extensions (RRID: SCR_002881 ).

claims.claim: Participants were recruited from the local population through advertisements and flyers.

evidence_by_agent.structure: Participants were recruited from the local population through advertisements on online blackboards at the University of Bonn and on local community websites, and through flyers posted in libraries, university cafeterias and sports facilities.

claims.claim: The fMRI data from four participants were excluded due to excessive head motion.

evidence_by_agent.structure: The fMRI data from four participants in Study 2 were excluded from the fMRI data analysis because of excessive head motion (>3 mm or >3°).

claims.claim: All statistical tests were two-tailed.
Bayes factors were calculated using default priors in JASP.

evidence_by_agent.structure: Bayes factors were calculated using default priors in JASP and express the probability of the data given H1 relative to H0 (BF10, values larger than one are in favour of H1).

claims.claim: The fMRI data were analysed using SPM12 software.

evidence_by_agent.structure: fMRI data were analysed using SPM12 software (RRID: SCR_007037 ; Wellcome Trust Centre for Neuroimaging, London, UK).

claims.claim: Functional connectivity analyses were performed using the gPPI toolbox for SPM.

evidence_by_agent.structure: We used the gPPI toolbox ( McLaren et al., 2012 ) for SPM to run seed-to-voxel functional connectivity analyses.

claims.claim: All clusters reported survive a significance threshold of p < 0.05 with family-wise error correction.

evidence_by_agent.structure: All clusters reported survive a significance threshold of p < 0.05 with family-wise error correction for multiple comparisons across the whole brain or a smaller volume when explicitly mentioned, based on an uncorrected voxel-wise (cluster-forming) threshold of p < 0.001.
